prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search procedure that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The authors propose to train on trial-and-error traces that include failed branches and backtracking decisions, and they instantiate this idea in intuitionistic propositional logic with a new Lean-formalized dataset, PropL. Empirically, they report that their model, TrialMaster, achieves higher out-of-distribution success rates and lower Lean-call cost than a conventional DFS-based prover trained only on successful proofs.

The paper’s central intuition is compelling. In theorem proving, failure is highly informative, and the discrepancy between “teacher-forced successful paths” during training and “search with many failed attempts” during inference is real. The paper also has a concrete systems contribution in constructing a dataset with explicit trial-and-error traces, which is genuinely useful because such data are scarce in public theorem proving corpora. The experimental results, especially the large gap between TrialMaster and the ablated model that uses the same inference style but is trained without trial-and-error traces, suggest that the signal is meaningful rather than purely an artifact of search hyperparameters. Overall, I found the paper interesting and potentially impactful, but there are several methodological and presentation issues that currently limit the strength of the claims.

The strongest aspect of the work is the clarity of the motivating problem. The paper identifies a training-inference mismatch that is easy to understand and plausibly general. The proposed remedy is also conceptually simple: expose the model to failed branches and backtracking behavior so that it can condition future decisions on prior failures. This is a good research direction, and the paper provides a concrete testbed where the hypothesis can be evaluated cleanly. The use of Lean for proof checking is another strength, since it ensures semantic correctness of accepted tactics and avoids ambiguity about whether generated proofs are valid.

The PropL dataset is potentially valuable, but the paper currently overstates some of its properties. In particular, the claim that the dataset is “complete, scalable, and representative” needs to be qualified much more carefully. The theorem space is restricted to intuitionistic propositional logic with bounded numbers of atoms and fixed formula size, and the proof traces are generated by a specific focused proof search procedure with a particular polarization scheme and an explicit incompleteness-inducing runtime heuristic. This means the dataset is representative of the distribution induced by the theorem generator and proof-search generator, not necessarily of theorem proving more broadly, nor even of all proof styles within intuitionistic propositional logic. The paper should distinguish between coverage of formulas under the chosen encoding and representativeness of proof behavior under the chosen search algorithm. Right now these notions are conflated.

A related concern is that the proof traces used for training and evaluation are all generated by the same deterministic or semi-random FPS-based procedure. This raises the possibility that TrialMaster is learning to imitate the idiosyncrasies of that search procedure, including its backtracking conventions and state numbering format, rather than learning a broadly useful notion of “reasoning from failure.” The fact that the model can emit syntactically correct backtrack instructions that refer to existing states is interesting, but it is not yet strong evidence of robust backtracking competence. It may simply reflect learning a formatting convention from homogeneous traces. A stronger evaluation would test transfer across proof generators, across different randomizations of the search policy, or at least across different trace serialization schemes.

The experimental design is promising but not yet fully convincing. The main comparison is between TrialMaster and a DFS baseline whose tactic generator is trained only on successful proofs. However, the two systems differ in more than just training data. TrialMaster performs autoregressive generation over the entire proof tree history and can emit explicit backtrack instructions, while the DFS baseline samples multiple tactics per state and relies on an external search controller. This makes the comparison somewhat entangled: it is not purely “training with failure vs training without failure,” but rather “a different model-plus-inference protocol vs a conventional search-based prover.” The ablation in Table 3 helps by comparing two models under the same inference style, and in my view this is actually the most important result in the paper. It should be elevated to the central experiment. As written, the headline comparison to DFS risks overstating what has been isolated.

Even within the DFS comparison, the baseline could be stronger and more carefully normalized. The paper varies temperature and number of sampled tactics, but it is not clear whether the baseline is tuned fairly under a fixed compute budget or fixed Lean-call budget. Since the paper emphasizes search cost, a more principled comparison would report success as a function of Lean calls, wall-clock time, or total model tokens generated. TrialMaster generates the entire proof path each step but only uses the first tactic; this may incur substantial language-model compute that is not reflected in the Lean-call metric. Conversely, DFS may make more Lean calls but less autoregressive generation per decision. If the claim is efficiency, Lean calls alone are not enough. At minimum, the paper should report total tokens generated, average prompt length, and inference latency. Otherwise the efficiency comparison is incomplete and potentially misleading.

The stopping criteria are also asymmetric in ways that deserve more scrutiny. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternatives after failed tactics at a state. This sounds unfavorable to TrialMaster, and the authors mention that the 1500-word limit is stricter for their method because it includes trial-and-error history. However, TrialMaster also benefits from directly modeling backtracking and from conditioning on the full serialized search history. More importantly, the 65-step cap for DFS appears somewhat ad hoc and is justified mainly by observed runtime growth at high temperatures. Since the paper’s main claim is about search efficiency, the evaluation should ideally compare methods under matched budgets rather than using a cap chosen around one baseline’s behavior. A success-versus-budget curve would be much more informative than a few operating points.

The out-of-distribution split is sensible in spirit, using proof length quantiles to separate train and test, but it is not entirely clear what kind of generalization is being measured. Because theorem statements all have the same number of internal nodes, and because proof traces are generated by the same algorithm, the OOD condition is primarily longer proofs under the same theorem distribution and proof style. That is a useful notion of extrapolation, but it is narrower than the paper sometimes suggests. It would help to characterize the train/test distributions more concretely: formula depth, connective frequencies, number of atoms, proof branching factor, average backtracking depth, and so on. Without this, it is hard to assess whether the gains come from better handling of longer contexts, better tactic selection, or better use of failure information per se.

The exploratory result that shorter trial-and-error traces outperform longer ones is interesting and potentially important. It suggests that not all failure data are equally useful, and that there may be an optimal amount or type of negative evidence. However, the current explanation is speculative. The paper should analyze what differs between “short” and “long” traces beyond length: are longer traces associated with harder theorems, noisier branches, more redundant failures, or different tactic distributions? This could lead to a stronger contribution around data curation, e.g., selecting informative failures rather than all failures.

There are also several missing ablations that would substantially strengthen the paper. First, compare training on successful proofs plus explicit error markers but without full failed branches, to isolate whether the benefit comes from negative examples, from richer sequential context, or from learning a backtracking token/action vocabulary. Second, compare against a model trained on successful proofs but prompted at inference with the same history format, including previously failed tactics, to test whether the gain is from training data or simply from richer prompting. Third, vary the amount of trial-and-error data per theorem: one trace, two traces, all ten traces, shortest versus random versus hardest. Fourth, test whether explicit backtrack instructions are necessary by replacing them with a simpler “history of failed tactics” representation. These ablations would clarify the mechanism behind the observed gains.

The paper’s claims about “learning backtracking without help from an external system” should also be softened. TrialMaster still relies on Lean to validate each tactic and to produce the next proof state, and the outer loop that feeds history back into the model is itself an external controller. What is true is that the model learns to emit backtrack instructions rather than relying on a separate DFS/BFS search policy. That is still interesting, but the current phrasing overstates autonomy.

Another issue is the narrowness of the domain. Intuitionistic propositional logic is a reasonable starting point because it allows controlled data generation and exact proof checking, but it is also a highly specialized setting with a small tactic vocabulary and relatively structured proof search. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but some of the broader framing around LLM theorem proving should be tempered. It remains unclear whether the same approach would help in richer domains where failures are more heterogeneous, proof states are larger, and tactic semantics are less local. The paper would benefit from explicitly positioning itself as a controlled study of the value of failure traces, rather than as evidence that this approach will broadly improve formal theorem proving.

Presentation quality is mixed. The core ideas are understandable, but the writing needs substantial polishing. There are many grammatical issues, awkward passive constructions, repeated sentences, and occasional imprecision in terminology. Some examples: the distinction between theorem generation and theorem proving is sometimes blurred; “uniformly sampled from all possible theorems” is too strong without careful conditioning on formula size and atom bound; and several claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence supports. The tables and figures are somewhat difficult to parse in the current form, and key quantitative results are missing from the text, especially for the OOD curves. The paper would benefit from a clearer exposition of the exact training examples, prompt formats, and serialization of proof trees. A concrete example of a TrialMaster input/output pair would help a lot.

I also have some technical questions that should be answered for reproducibility and interpretation. How exactly are proof states serialized for the model? Are theorem statements included at every step or only initially? What tokenizer and maximum context length are used, and how does the “1500-word” limit map to model tokens? Are the two selected training traces per theorem fixed once or resampled each epoch? How many total training sequences result from the 109,887 theorems? What is the variance across random seeds for fine-tuning and inference? Since the reported differences are sometimes modest against the best DFS setting, confidence intervals or multiple runs would be useful. It would also help to know how often TrialMaster emits backtrack instructions, how often those lead to eventual success, and whether the model ever loops or revisits states unnecessarily.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has a solid core idea and encouraging empirical evidence. The dataset contribution is useful, and the ablation comparing identical inference with and without trial-and-error training is particularly compelling. If the authors can tighten the claims, improve the fairness and completeness of the evaluation, and better isolate the source of the gains, this could become a strong paper.

My overall assessment is moderately positive. The paper is novel in a meaningful way, addresses an important mismatch in theorem-proving systems, and presents promising results in a controlled formal domain. However, the current version falls short of fully substantiating its broader claims because of confounded comparisons, incomplete efficiency accounting, and overstatement of dataset representativeness and learned backtracking ability. I would encourage acceptance only if the venue is comfortable with a focused empirical study in a narrow domain and if the authors can address at least some of the evaluation concerns in revision.

The most important improvements I would recommend are: make the same-inference ablation the centerpiece; add budget-matched comparisons and token/latency costs; clarify and soften claims about completeness, representativeness, and autonomous backtracking; provide more detail on data generation and prompt formatting; and add ablations that isolate which aspects of trial-and-error supervision matter most. With these changes, the paper would be substantially stronger and more convincing.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies whether large language models for theorem proving benefit from training on trial-and-error proof traces rather than only successful proof paths. To enable this, the authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proofs generated by a focused proof search procedure that records both successful and failed/backtracked steps. They fine-tune Llama-2-7B in two settings: a conventional tactic generator trained on correct proofs only and TrialMaster trained on proof trees containing trial-and-error information. On their benchmark, TrialMaster achieves similar near-perfect in-distribution performance and substantially better out-of-distribution success rate than the proof-only baseline, while using fewer Lean calls than strong DFS baselines. The paper argues that exposure to failed search paths helps the model learn better tactic selection and backtracking behavior.
strengths: The paper addresses a real mismatch between training and inference in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful trajectories but used inside search procedures that repeatedly encounter failures.
The proposed dataset contribution is meaningful within its scope: PropL is Lean-checkable, includes trial-and-error traces, and appears systematically generated rather than manually curated.
The empirical comparison is clear at a high level and shows a sizable OOD improvement for the trial-and-error-trained model over a proof-only ablation (88.7% vs. 59.3%).
The work evaluates both success rate and search cost, which is important for theorem proving systems where efficiency matters as much as raw solve rate.
The paper includes an ablation isolating the effect of trial-and-error supervision and an exploratory analysis on proof length, both of which help support the central claim.
weaknesses: The experimental domain is very narrow: intuitionistic propositional logic with synthetic proofs generated by a fixed search algorithm. It is unclear how much the conclusions transfer to richer theorem proving settings.
The comparison is not fully apples-to-apples because TrialMaster and the DFS baseline use materially different inference mechanisms, stopping criteria, and interaction patterns with Lean.

The dataset generation and theorem sampling claims are stronger than what is convincingly justified; in particular, the notion of being 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems' and 'representative' is underspecified and potentially misleading.
The proof search generator is intentionally incomplete due to an added runtime assumption, which weakens claims of completeness and may bias the training/evaluation distribution.
Results lack statistical rigor: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple training runs despite stochastic proof generation and model fine-tuning.
The baseline set is limited. There is no comparison to stronger modern search-based or error-aware methods beyond the authors' own proof-only variants.
The paper claims the model learns backtracking, but the evidence provided is weak: correct formatting of backtrack instructions does not establish semantically effective backtracking behavior.
methodological_flaws: There is a scientific-logic mismatch in the main comparison: TrialMaster performs greedy one-step generation with explicit backtrack tokens conditioned on full history, whereas the baseline is a DFS system sampling multiple tactics per state with tuned temperature and branching factor. Because both training data and inference algorithms differ, the gains cannot be attributed cleanly to trial-and-error training alone.

The paper claims PropL is 'complete, scalable, and representative,' but also states that the proof search procedure is made incomplete by forbidding an implication from being used to show its own premise. This directly undermines the completeness claim.

The theorem-generation argument conflates a bijection between natural numbers and formulas with uniform sampling over the space of theorems. A bijection only gives an enumeration; without a precise finite support or distribution over formula size and validity, 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems' is mathematically ill-posed.

The train/test split may induce distributional artifacts unrelated to theorem difficulty. Splitting by proof-length quantiles computed from the same deterministic/procedural prover can favor models that imitate that prover's style rather than genuinely generalize in logic.

The evaluation protocol is asymmetric. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, while DFS can continue exploring alternative tactics at a state after failures. Conversely, TrialMaster's backtrack instructions do not incur Lean calls, making N_Lean not a fully comparable measure of total inference cost across systems.

The evidence for empirical validity is incomplete because only single-run point estimates are reported. Given stochastic selection of training proofs and stochastic decoding in DFS baselines, variance could materially affect the reported margins, especially the small differences against the strongest DFS settings.

The claim that the model performs backtracking 'without help from an external system' is overstated: Lean still validates every non-backtrack tactic and the prompting mechanism explicitly maintains the proof tree/history externally. This is not autonomous internal backtracking in a strict sense.
